idiom_name: interface Implementor plus an abstract class holding it, wired by DI
implementation_notes: The implementor is an interface (a nominal contract; members are public and abstract by default) and the abstraction is an abstract class - or a plain class with a primary-constructor parameter - holding it, normally injected through the constructor; the compiler enforces the contract, so both hierarchies are ordinary C# types and no forwarding boilerplate beyond the abstraction's own methods is needed. What replaces the classic structure in modern code is constructor injection wired by Microsoft.Extensions.DependencyInjection (optionally with keyed services), so the concrete implementor is chosen at startup instead of by the abstraction. Interfaces cannot hold instance state, which is why sharing implementor state means sharing the concrete instance through DI rather than through an abstract base; the classic abstract-class-plus-interface shape is still justified when refined abstractions add operations that share the same primitives.
pitfalls: Default interface members (C# 8+) put behaviour in the contract: an implementor that forgets to override silently inherits it, hiding the fact that the primitive was never implemented.

Several registrations of one interface resolve to the last one (or to IEnumerable<T>), so binding the wrong implementor is a configuration accident rather than a compile error - use keyed services when implementors coexist.

Interfaces cannot hold instance state: shared implementor state must live in a registered singleton, and a static field in a concrete implementor makes that state process-wide and defeats independent variation.
